name: Marder 1A3

placement_rationale.text: Marder's own characteristics list an effective cannon range of ~1,100 m — an autocannon engagement envelope, not a distance an IFV sits at while waiting to commit. 6 km in the near-operational band reflects the vehicle's actual employment: per its own contrast_vs_traditional note, getting infantry to a position increasingly means dismounting short of the objective and moving the final stretch on foot, so the IFV itself holds further back than a hull-down tank would, inside doctrine.md's close-reconnaissance depth (1–5 km) but not at its inner edge. (Nudged 6→6.4 km from this category's shared round-number value so it doesn't literally coincide with side_a-armor-m1126-icv-stryker on the map's distance axis — a small, deterministic spread within the same band, not a new plausibility claim beyond what's already argued above.)

characteristics: Strength: Well-proven Cold War IFV design, integrated ATGM gives organic anti-armor capability beyond the autocannon
Limitation: Aging design (1970s) relative to newer IFVs donated to Ukraine; aluminium armor lighter than modern composite types
Estimated quantity available: Donated in the dozens; exact current total not fully disclosed
employment_notes: One of the earliest Western IFVs delivered (2023), used to reinforce mechanized infantry as Soviet-legacy BMP stocks depleted
contrast_vs_traditional: Marder doctrine paired IFVs with tanks in a combined-arms breakthrough, using armor to protect dismounting infantry at the objective. On a front where a moving column is exactly what persistent drone ISR is built to find, getting infantry to a position increasingly means dismounting well short of it and moving the last stretch on foot under cover — the IFV's armor now protects the approach, not the arrival.

sources.label: Army Recognition — Marder 1A3 first combat mission in Ukraine
